blocks.x: Core definitions
Atom Democritus (~500 BC) first suggested the particulate nature of matter, calling the basic units of elements atoms. Aristotle disagreed, proposing matter was continuous ("Hyle").
Orbital A volume of space around the nucleus within which there is a 95% probability of finding an electron — the wave function (ψ) in atoms.
Valence electrons Outermost electrons involved in bond formation; they have high energy. Core electrons sit between the nucleus and valence electrons and do not bond.
Atomic models→ Quantum numbers→ Electron config.→ Periodic table→ Periodic properties
Evolution of atomic models

c: Solid sphere / small indivisible hard-ball model

blocks.x: History of atomic theory
From philosophical speculation to experimentally-tested quantum models — each new model fixed a flaw in the one before it.
Before Dalton
Suggested the particulate nature of matter, calling the basic units of elements atoms.
Proposed matter was continuous and not composed of smaller particles, naming it Hyle.
Dalton's atomic theory

John Dalton was the first to put forward a scientific theory on the physical and chemical properties of the atom, based on the law of definite proportion (Proust) and the law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier).

items: Elements consist of small indivisible particles called atoms.
Atoms can neither be created nor destroyed.
Atoms of the same element are identical — identical mass/size and the same physical and chemical properties.
Atoms combine to form compounds in simple ratios.

blocks.title: Dalton's theory — where it was later found incorrect

items: Indivisibility of atoms: the existence of sub-atomic particles — protons, neutrons and electrons — disproved this.
Impossibility of creating atoms: via radioactivity and fusion reactions, new atoms can be formed.
Presence of isotopes: atoms of the same element can have different masses, e.g. hydrogen-3 isotopes — ¹₁H protium, ²₁H deuterium, ³₁H tritium.

blocks.x: Thomson's plum-pudding model

J. J. Thomson proposed the "plum pudding" (watermelon) model, developed from his cathode ray experiment: a cathode ray tube fires charged particles from a cathode toward an anode; an electric field deflects the ray, revealing that the atom contains smaller, negatively-charged particles embedded in a positive "pudding".
Rutherford's nuclear atom model
Ernest Rutherford's alpha-scattering (gold foil) experiment fired a beam of α-particles at thin gold foil.

items: Most α-particles travelled through the foil undeflected.
Some α-particles were deflected by small angles.
Occasionally, an α-particle travelled back from the foil.

blocks.x: This led to the nuclear atom model: a tiny, dense, positively-charged nucleus with electrons orbiting around it.
Bohr's planetary model

blocks.title: Why electrons don't spiral into the nucleus

blocks.x: From Rutherford's model, electrons were thought to orbit the nucleus at high speed. Scientists wondered why the negative electrons did not lose energy and spiral into the nucleus. This was explained by the quantum theory, of which Niels Bohr, a Danish physicist, was a chief advocate.
Using the hydrogen atom, Bohr suggested an electron could not have just any energy but is restricted to permissible energy levels — electrons exist in discrete energy levels.

Bohr's study was facilitated by examining spectra. A line spectrum is observed when hydrogen atoms are given energy by passing an electric current through them at low pressure, or when heated in a flame. He explained that electrons are arranged in energy levels around the nucleus, revolving in definite orbits — like planets orbiting the sun.

Only specific energy values were permissible for the orbits, so the energy of the electron was quantised. Each orbit was assigned a number called the principal quantum number, a whole number from 1 to infinity.
The wave-mechanistic model

Bohr's model could not account for the line spectra of elements bigger than hydrogen. It treated the electron as a particle, but Louis de Broglie, a French graduate student, suggested electrons also have wave properties (momentum and wavelength) — the wave-particle dual nature of the electron.

blocks.title: The uncertainty principle & the Schrödinger equation

blocks.x: Problem: for a sub-atomic particle, it is not possible to know its position (wavelength) and momentum at the same time.
Postulation — the uncertainty principle (Werner Heisenberg): it is difficult to determine the position and momentum of an electron at the same time.

Erwin Schrödinger combined de Broglie's equation with others for wave motion to derive the Schrödinger equation, describing an electron's behaviour in a hydrogen atom (the equation is complicated for more than one electron).

items: The solutions of the equation are the wave functions, Psi (ψ).
ψ² is a mathematical expression of the probability of finding an electron in a small volume that varies from place to place.
The wave function in atoms is called an orbital — a volume of space around the nucleus with a 95% probability of finding an electron.
Bohr's model considered only one quantum number; the wave-mechanics model considers two additional quantum numbers.

Quantum mechanics of the atom
Four quantum numbers uniquely describe every electron in an atom; three rules govern how electrons fill the available orbitals.
What each one describes

Principal quantum number (n) Determines the energy level and closeness of electrons to the nucleus. Naming starts with K, L, M, N… The maximum number of electrons per shell is 2n². A shell is a collection of orbitals with the same principal quantum number.
Orbital / azimuthal quantum number (l) Defines the shape of an orbital. Ranges from 0 to n−1. When n = 1, l = 0 (s-orbital) — symmetrically spherical, holding up to two electrons.
Magnetic quantum number (mₗ) Describes the orientation of orbitals in space. Ranges from −l to +l, including zero.
Spin quantum number (mₛ) Represents the ability of electrons to spin about their axis, clockwise or anti-clockwise. Values range from −½ to +½.
Orbital shapes by azimuthal quantum number
Quantum numbers for n = 1–4
Electronic configuration — three governing rules
Electrons must first fill the orbitals of lower energies before orbitals of higher energies — this applies to all approaches.
Filling order: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f…
Sodium (₁₁Na): first approach (octet rule) = 2, 8, 1. Second approach (all quantum numbers) = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹.
The total number of electrons that can fill an orbital must be two, and these electrons must have opposite spins (the second approach).
Example — Lithium (₃Li) = 1s² 2s¹; Boron (₅B) = 1s² 2s² 2pₓ¹ 2py 2pz.
Degenerate orbitals (orbitals of the same energy) are first filled singly and with parallel spins before pairing up with opposite spins.
Example — Nitrogen (₇N) = 1s² 2s² 2pₓ¹ 2py¹ 2pz¹ (each 2p orbital singly filled); Oxygen (₈O) = 1s² 2s² 2pₓ² 2py¹ 2pz¹ (one 2p orbital now paired).
Configurations for elements with Z > 20
Note: Cr and Cu deviate from the simple filling order because half-filled and fully-filled 3d subshells are extra stable.
Periodicity
Mendeleev, a Russian chemist, put forward the modern form of the periodic table, arranged by the periodicity of atoms' electronic structure and by atomic number.
Groups, periods and blocks
Groups

Vertical arrangement. Elements in a group share the same valence electrons or similar atomic configurations. There are 8 main groups. In most elements, the number of valence electrons equals the group number.
Periods
Horizontal arrangement. The period number is the main energy level occupied by the valence electron. There are 7 periods; atomic number rises by 1 across a period.
Blocks
Groups of elements whose valence electrons occupy the same orbital type: s, p, d, f blocks.
Shared valence electrons, shared behaviour

Where group members share similar physical and chemical properties, they can be considered "a family" — for example, alkali metals (Li, Na, K) and halogens (F, Cl, Br, I). Elements in the same group have different n-numbers (principal quantum numbers), e.g. ₃Li = [He] 2s¹, ₁₁Na = [Ne] 3s¹, ₁₉K = [Ar] 4s¹.
Exception: Group 4 is not a true family — it contains both carbon (a non-metal) and silicon (a metalloid), which do not behave alike.
How many elements fit in each period

To prevent a clumsy arrangement, elements whose valence electron fills the 4f-orbitals are placed in a separate row at the bottom — the Lanthanides (Lanthanum → Lutetium). Those filling 5f-orbitals sit below them — the Actinides (Actinium → Lawrencium).
s, p, d and f blocks
Groups 1 & 2 — valence electrons in s-orbitals.
Groups 3–8 of the second period onward (B, C, N, O, F, Ne…) — valence electrons in p-orbitals.
Valence electrons fill d-orbitals. 4th period: Sc–Zn (1st transition series); 5th period: Y–Cd (2nd series); 6th period: La–Hg (3rd series).
Valence electrons fill f-orbitals — the Lanthanides and Actinides. Note: s and p blocks are the main group elements.
Trends across the table

Physical and chemical properties that reoccur across the periodic table, driven by common features of electronic structure: atomic/ionic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity.
Effective nuclear charge & screening
The net attraction of a proton in the nucleus for the valence electrons. It increases across the period.
The decreased attraction of protons for the valence electrons, caused by core electrons. It increases down the group.
Atomic radius

Half the distance between two bonded nuclei in a molecule (r = ½ × d). Atomic size depends on how strongly the nucleus attracts the valence electrons: greater attraction → smaller atom, so size decreases across a period. From halogens to rare gases there is an increase in atomic size due to repulsion among electrons in the outer shell.
Ionic radius
Smaller than the parent atom (e.g. Li → Li⁺, isoelectronic with He). Cations have fewer electrons than protons, increasing effective nuclear charge. Decreases across a period, increases down a group.
Larger than the parent atom (e.g. F → F⁻, isoelectronic with Ne). More electrons than protons increases the screening effect. Increases across a period, decreases down a group.
Ionization energy (Eᵢ)

The energy required to remove the most loosely-bound electron from a gaseous atom, forming one mole of gaseous cation. Determinants: atomic radius, penetrative effect, shielding/screening effect, and stability of electronic configuration.
Eᵢ increases — atomic radius decreases, screening stays roughly the same, and penetrative effect increases, so more energy is needed to remove valence electrons.
Eᵢ decreases — atomic radius and screening effect increase while penetrative effect decreases, so less energy is needed to remove valence electrons.

items: Beryllium > Boron: Be = 1s² 2s² has a fully-filled, stable 2s subshell; B = 1s² 2s² 2p¹ has a 2p electron at a higher, less stable energy level (2s electrons also have greater penetrative power).

Nitrogen > Oxygen: N's 2p orbitals are half-filled (2p³), spreading electrons out and reducing repulsion — very stable. O's 2p⁴ has two paired electrons in one orbital, causing repulsion and instability, lowering its Eᵢ.
Noble gases require unusually high ionization energy due to the exceptional stability of their full-shell configuration.

blocks.x: Electron affinity (Eₐ)
The amount of energy change (released) when an electron is added to a gaseous atom.

The second electron added to oxygen faces a repulsive force from the already-negative ion, requiring energy input — a positive electron affinity value. Down a group, Eₐ decreases (less attraction for added electrons, larger atoms, lower effective nuclear charge); across a period, Eₐ increases.

blocks.title: Discrepancy: fluorine's surprisingly low (less negative) Eₐ

blocks.x: Fluorine's very small size creates a very strong repulsive field for any incoming electron, giving it a less negative Eₐ than expected.
Period 2 discrepancy: B (−27 kJ/mol) < C (−122 kJ/mol), but N = 0 kJ/mol — nitrogen's half-filled, stable 2p³ configuration resists adding another electron.
Electronegativity (EN)

The ability of an atom in a molecule to attract bonded/shared electrons to itself. The main determinant is atomic radius: the smaller the atom, the higher its electronegativity. Unlike electron affinity (measured directly for gaseous isolated atoms), electronegativity is measured indirectly on a comparative scale — Pauling's scale — and has no unit.
4.0highest electronegativity on Pauling's scale — fluorine 0.7lowest electronegativity on Pauling's scale — francium 2families at the extremes: halogens (most EN) vs. alkali metals (least EN)
How the four properties trend together
Atomic size↓ across, ↑ down group
Ionization E.↑ across, ↓ down group
Electronegativity↑ across, ↓ down group
Across a period atomic size shrinks while electronegativity and ionization energy climb; down a group the reverse holds — atoms grow larger, and both properties fall.
